prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, trapping many neutral atoms at the magic wavelength to reach accuracy and stability at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I have moved from IceCube (B029) to optical lattice clocks (B042) with Katori and Ye. The round-1 exchange removed the two reasons I ranked clocks fifth. My objection was that the lattice clock refines a capability created by the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize on control of single quantum systems. Kroll's reply, supported by Lindroth and Johansson, is that neither prize covered a many-atom, light-shift-cancelled lattice: Katori's magic-wavelength condition lets thousands of atoms sit in the Lamb-Dicke regime without Doppler or recoil broadening, and that architecture, not the comb or the single ion, is what took the field to 1e-18. As an experimentalist who builds detectors, I judge that a new measurement principle realised at record performance, not a polishing of an old one. Lindroth asked whether agreement among atomic-physics members is bias, and Olsson asked whether my ranking reflected physics or a view on timing. It is neither: I am outside AMO, and my remaining hesitation was about discovery character, not about the quality of the work. The maturity is the best on the shortlist, with independent groups reproducing 1e-18 uncertainties across Sr, Yb and Hg and comparing clocks between institutions. The credit is two identifiable people, the originator of the concept and the leader of the group that set the performance standard, with no leadership-proxy problem. I would write the citation around the lattice architecture and its demonstrated 1e-18 performance, so that it stands whatever the metrology bodies decide about the second, and so that it does not lean on the comb or the thorium nuclear clock.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is real, and the committee should not dismiss it. A reader can fairly say that optical frequency metrology has now been honoured three times. The credit boundary is also not fully closed: Takamoto and Ido (first Sr lattice-clock demonstration) and Lemonde (early Sr comparisons) lie outside the two names, and I cannot settle the priority question from the supplied evidence. A two-name prize is defensible only if the citation is explicit that it honours the concept and the record performance. Ye's claim also draws partly on comb and ultrastable-laser work, which the citation must keep out. Finally, this is an instrument-driven achievement that improves a measurement rather than a discovery of nature in the sense Danielsson weighs most; if the committee puts that criterion first, B026 or B029 would reasonably outrank it. I give that criterion less weight than I did in round 1, but I do not regard it as empty.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock is a new principle, not a refinement of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and that the citation should rest on demonstrated lattice clocks at 1e-18 and inter-laboratory comparisons, not on the pending redefinition of the second.
responses.response: Your answer to my overlap objection is the argument that moved me. The comb is a ruler and the single ion is a different physical system, and neither supplies the many-atom, light-shift-cancelled architecture. I accept that as a distinct principle. I also agree on the citation: it should rest on what has been shown, so that it does not depend on a metrological timetable. I would add one drafting requirement beyond your wording. The text should name the lattice and the 1e-18 performance explicitly, so that neither Ye's comb work nor the thorium clock is credited by implication. Your point that Takamoto, Ido and Lemonde are an open question stays open for me, and the citation cannot cure it.

responses.point: Lindroth warns that agreement among members with an atomic-physics vantage is not itself evidence of merit, and asks whether colleagues outside AMO find the conceptual step substantial. She also says IceCube is less settled than clocks on maturity and that a source-identification paper could change that.
responses.response: I take the warning seriously, and I cannot be counted among the AMO members: I come from particle and astroparticle instrumentation. From that outside position I find the conceptual step substantial, because the magic-wavelength condition solves a trapping problem that would otherwise block a many-atom clock, and the 1e-18 result has been reproduced independently, which is the test I would apply to any detector claim. On IceCube I accept your maturity comparison. The diffuse flux is secure, but the sources are largely unresolved. Waiting for the source-identification work you describe would cost the field little, so I no longer press B029 now.

responses.point: Danielsson keeps the Higgs discovery (B026) first because nature answered a half-century question, because the 2013 prize honoured only the theory, and because Nobel committees have always had to name three people for collective efforts. He would not object strongly if the committee settled on Katori and Ye.
responses.response: I agree that the Higgs observation has the greatest scientific weight on the shortlist, and that the 2013 prize did not cover the experiment. I part company on the sentence that Nobel committees have always had to name three people. In earlier collective cases the credited individuals could be tied to a specific idea or decisive act. The chair's round-1 question asks whether any member can say what Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee each contributed to the 2012 observation, and I have not seen an answer. Your own file says that if no defensible three names exist the committee should turn elsewhere. I think that condition is met for now, and your willingness to accept Katori and Ye is the reason I now regard B042 as reachable by agreement on the science, not by default.

responses.point: Olsson asked whether my fifth-place ranking of the clocks reflected a physics concern or a view that metrology should be rewarded only after the redefinition of the second, and she argues that a prize for the invention should not wait for a metrological decision.
responses.response: It was a physics concern, about overlap with the comb and ion-control prizes and about discovery character, and it was never about the redefinition. I agree with you that the prize is for the invention and the demonstrated sub-1e-18 comparisons, and that tying our judgement to a bureaucratic timetable would be a mistake. Having heard Kroll and Johansson on the novelty of the lattice architecture, I no longer hold the overlap concern as decisive. Your point that Takamoto and Ido are a real but secondary priority question is the right handling. I would settle it in the citation wording and in the committee record, not by adding a third name that Katori's concept and Ye's performance work do not require.

uncertainties: Whether Takamoto, Ido and Lemonde have a first-demonstration or comparison claim that a two-name credit leaves unrecognised; I cannot resolve this from the supplied evidence and I am relying on memory of the literature.
Whether the committee accepts the many-atom magic-wavelength lattice as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or sees clocks as a third prize for optical frequency metrology.

Whether the case for IceCube (B029) would strengthen enough in the coming years, with a second compelling source identification and a settled population origin for the diffuse flux, to overtake clocks; I would revisit it then.
Whether the committee can write a citation for Ye that rests on the lattice clock and not on the comb, the ultrastable lasers or the thorium nuclear clock.

Whether my change from B029 to B042 reflects the scientific argument or the pull of the strongest block of support; I have tried to base it on the novelty and maturity arguments and not on the support count.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I no longer prefer B029, so my Fermi-LAT, PAMELA and PoGO+ collaboration-level link to the TXS 0506+056 follow-up is no longer attached to my preferred configuration. It would matter again if the committee turned to B029, and in that case I would leave the question of my recusal to the committee. I have no documented personal or institutional tie to Katori or Ye, or to any other shortlisted candidate. I do not claim any knowledge of confidential committee matters.
